newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican corporate bonds seen as good buy-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexican corporate bonds seen as good buy-analysts.

text.p: Argentine companies may have better fundamentals, but with the continued improvement in the Mexican economy, many analysts are saying that Mexican corporate Eurobonds could present a better buy.
"Argentines are a better credit quality and are a little more transparent, but Mexican companies have been through a lot," said Santander Investment debt analyst Jim Garvey.
"I don't see a lot of downside risk right now. There will be a slow continual improvement," he said.
Added Bankers Trust economist Christopher Taylor, "I think that Argentine companies in general have stronger fundamentals, but the spread on Argentine bonds are already tight."
"If I can get 11.0 percent on Mexico and 9.5 percent on Argentina I will go for Mexico even if Argentine companies are stronger," Taylor said.
Spreads have tightened on the Mexican corporate debt recently, as, among other things, the strengthening of the Mexican economy has given heart to investors.
Gross domestic product grew by 7.2 percent in the second quarter of this year, although compared to a weak second quarter a year earlier.
Much of the growth in the economy has come from a booming export sector, with domestic demand still week.
In a recent Reuters survey, economists forecast GDP growth of 4.08 percent in 1996.
"People are more comfortable with the Mexican outlook as the recovery strengthens," Taylor said.
Even with severe cash-flow problems, many companies were able to survive the deep downturn.
Moreover, economists say the underlying causes of the crash -- such as a huge current account deficit and an unbalanced debt structure -- have been addressed to a large extent.
But Mexican companies are faced with a large amount of maturing paper in 1997 and 1998.
"There were a lot of three and five-year bonds issued a few years ago, and there has not been a lot of new debt since then," Garvey said.
About $1.5 billion worth will have to be retired in 1997 and about $2.4 billion in 1998.

"It won't be problem if they (companies) are proactive. I think it will be a problem if they wait until a month before they are due. But a lot of the companies are starting to raise money now," Taylor said.
For example, cement maker Cemex has made a tender offer for $1.0 billion of its paper coming due in 1998.
